title: The 'Promising Failure' of the First Car to Carry Ferrari's Name
dek: In May 1947 the first Ferrari retired from its debut race while leading; Enzo Ferrari, whose rushed first car had failed in 1940, called it promising.

story.event: Building the 125 S, the first car under his own name, and its debut retirement at Piacenza
story.summary: Dismissed by Alfa Romeo in 1939 and barred for four years from racing under his own name, Enzo Ferrari funded a small Modena firm from his settlement and savings; its rushed 1940 car failed, and during the war it made machine tools at Maranello. Against a friend's warning that he was giving up a profitable business, he commissioned a V12 from Gioachino Colombo in 1945; the resulting 125 S retired while leading its debut at Piacenza on 11 May 1947, which he called a promising failure, and won the Rome Grand Prix on 25 May.
paragraphs: On 11 May 1947, at a race circuit in Piacenza, the first car ever to carry Enzo Ferrari's name was leading when its fuel pump broke. Franco Cortese had to pull the little 125 S out of the race. Ferrari called it "a promising failure".

He had reason to know one kind of failure from another. Through the 1930s his Scuderia Ferrari ran Alfa Romeo's racing, and he then led Alfa's own racing department until Alfa ended his contract in September 1939. Under the terms of his exit he could not, for four years, rebuild the Scuderia or put the Ferrari name on a racing car. "With the settlement after my twenty years and with my savings I transformed the Scuderia into a small car factory," he later wrote. Its first car, built for the 1940 Mille Miglia under the name Auto Avio Costruzioni, took four months from design to delivery. Both cars entered retired. The attempt ended in failure, Ferrari said, "largely because the car had been built too hastily."

During the war, under rules that pushed industry out of the cities, he moved the business in 1943 to land he owned at Maranello, where it made machine tools; the factory was bombed in November 1944 and again that winter, and was quickly rebuilt. In 1945 Ferrari asked Gioachino Colombo, who had designed Alfa's 158 racing car, for a 12-cylinder engine of about 1.5 litres. When he told Cortese he meant to go back to building racing cars, his friend was blunt: "You'd have to be crazy to give up a business as profitable as this." Ferrari went ahead. The car first ran on 12 March 1947, still without its bodywork.

The verdict on Piacenza held. On 25 May, a fortnight after the retirement, Cortese drove the 125 S to victory in the Rome Grand Prix on the streets around the Baths of Caracalla, more than ten seconds ahead of a Maserati. Wins followed that summer at Vercelli, Vigevano and Varese, and in July Tazio Nuvolari won with the car at Forlì and Parma. The first Ferrari grand prix car appeared in September 1948.

quote.text: as in races it is not the large stride or high lift that makes the speed; so in business, the keeping close to the matter, and not taking of it too much at once, procureth dispatch.
quote.source_title: The Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral, Project Gutenberg eBook #575
quote.connection: Ferrari's four-month car of 1940 failed, he said, from haste; the 125 S came after more than a year of work and then raced thirteen times in four months. Bacon, reaching for a racing image himself, says real speed comes from steady stride rather than lunging.

reflection: Ferrari had two failures to compare. The 1940 car was built in four months and, by his own account, failed because it was rushed. The 1947 car failed because one part broke while it was in front. Both ended in a retirement, but only one told him that the way he had worked was wrong.

When something you have made goes badly, it helps to ask which kind of failure it was before deciding what it means. A part that gave way can often be fixed within a fortnight. Work that was rushed asks you to slow down, and slowing down is not the same as giving up.
invitation: Think of the last piece of work that disappointed you. Write one sentence saying whether it failed because it was rushed or because one part gave way, and let that sentence decide your next step.

sources.title: Enzo Ferrari's Auto Avio Costruzioni Tipo 815: the story of the true 'first Ferraris' (Karl Ludvigsen)
sources.supports: Alfa Romeo ended Ferrari's contract on 6 September 1939; a clause barred him for four years from rebuilding the Scuderia or being involved in racing; Ferrari's own words 'With the settlement after my twenty years and with my savings I transformed the Scuderia into a small car factory'; Auto Avio Costruzioni founded September 1939 at the former Scuderia base in Modena; the Tipo 815 built for the 1940 Mille Miglia, agreed at Christmas 1939 with four months to go; both cars retired; Ferrari's verdict that it ended in failure 'largely because the car had been built too hastily'.

sources.title: Three colours red: How Ferrari, Maserati and Alfa Romeo dominated postwar grand prix racing (Richard Williams, July 2014)
sources.supports: Under wartime decentralisation rules Ferrari moved from Modena to land he owned at Maranello; the factory was bombed twice in the closing weeks of 1944 and kept making machine tools (milling machines) with the prancing horse badge; Cortese's warning 'You'd have to be crazy to give up a business as profitable as this'; the first Ferrari appeared in March 1947 after more than a year of work, with Colombo's 1.5-litre V12; Piacenza debut that May; first win at the Terme di Caracalla in Rome, then Vercelli, Vigevano and Varese; Nuvolari's wins at Forlì and Parma in July.

sources.title: History of Enzo Ferrari (company timeline), Internet Archive copy of January 2016
sources.supports: Scuderia Ferrari as Alfa Romeo's racing outpost from 1933; Ferrari head of Alfa Corse until he left on 6 September 1939 on condition he not use the Ferrari name with races or racing cars for at least four years; Auto Avio Costruzioni opened on 13 September 1939 at the old Scuderia premises in Modena; two 815s for the 1940 Mille Miglia that failed to shine; move to Maranello in 1943 and production mainly of grinding machines; factory bombed on 4 November 1944 and again the following February and quickly rebuilt; work on the first Ferrari with a V12 begun in late 1945; the 125 S first taken out on 12 March 1947.

sources.title: Rome 1947: the first 100% Ferrari victory (24 April 2019), Internet Archive copy
sources.supports: Ferrari commissioned Gioachino Colombo in mid-1945; the 12-cylinder 125 engine first ran on 12 March 1947 without bodywork, between Maranello and Formigine; track debut at Piacenza on 11 May 1947, retiring from the lead with a broken fuel pump; 'A promising failure'; Rome Grand Prix around the Baths of Caracalla on 25 May 1947, won by Franco Cortese more than ten seconds ahead of Guido Barbieri's Maserati.

sources.title: Ferrari 125 S (1947), Internet Archive copy
sources.supports: The 125 S as the first car to wear the Ferrari badge; V12 designed by Colombo; Enzo Ferrari's own description of the Piacenza debut as 'a promising failure'; Cortese pulled out with a fuel-pump problem while leading; 13 races in the following four months.

sources.title: In the beginning... (April 1997)
sources.supports: The 1940 Auto Avio Costruzioni 815 was not badged Ferrari because of a contractual obligation to Alfa Romeo; Ferrari engaged Gioachino Colombo, designer of the Alfetta 158, for a small-capacity V12.

sources.title: The mantle of mystique: Denis Jenkinson's tribute to Enzo Ferrari (October 1988)
sources.supports: Ferrari ran Alfa Romeo's racing under the Scuderia Ferrari banner in the 1930s; in 1947 he struck out on his own as a manufacturer; wartime work for the Italian government enabled a new factory at Maranello; Colombo designed the first Ferrari V12.

sources.title: The first Prancing Horsepower (Paolo d'Alessio, April 2006)
sources.supports: In 1946 Ferrari announced a sports car and a grand prix car, both with V12 engines; the first Ferrari grand prix car appeared at the Italian Grand Prix in Turin on 5 September 1948.

sources.title: The real first Ferrari: Frankel's insight
sources.supports: The AAC 815 was so named because of a four-year condition in Ferrari's release from Alfa Romeo; it took four months from design to delivery; both cars entered the 1940 Mille Miglia (Brescia Grand Prix) and failed to finish.

cross_checks.claim: Ferrari's departure from Alfa Romeo came with a four-year bar, so his first car (1940) could not carry his name.
The 1940 Auto Avio Costruzioni 815 took about four months to build and both cars retired from the Mille Miglia.
During the war the business moved to Maranello, made machine tools, and was bombed but rebuilt.
Ferrari commissioned Gioachino Colombo to design a 1.5-litre V12 for the first Ferrari.
The 125 S retired from the lead at Piacenza on 11 May 1947 with a fuel-pump failure, which Enzo Ferrari called a promising failure.
Franco Cortese won the Rome Grand Prix at the Baths of Caracalla in the 125 S, the first Ferrari victory.
The 125 S first ran on 12 March 1947.

research_notes: Year of leaving Alfa Romeo: Karl Ludvigsen (Revs Institute) dates Alfa's termination letter to 6 September 1939 and quotes Ferrari's 'In 1939 came my divorce from Alfa Romeo'; Goodwood says he escaped his Alfa contract in 1938, and Denis Jenkinson (Motor Sport, 1988) dates the falling-out with Alfa's chief engineer to 1938 while saying Ferrari ran Alfa's racing until 1939. The story uses September 1939 for the end of the contract. The 815: Ferrari's memoir is said (Goodwood) to claim one car was built, but both Ludvigsen and Goodwood document two cars entered, so the story says both retired. Machine tools: Motor Sport (2014) says milling machines; Ferrari's 2016 company timeline says grinding machines copied from German tools, so the story says machine tools. Bombing: Ferrari's timeline gives 4 November 1944 and the following February; Motor Sport (2014) says twice in the closing weeks of 1944; the story follows Ferrari's dates. Commission date: Ferrari's 2019 magazine says Colombo was asked in mid-1945 and its 2016 timeline says design work began in late 1945; the story says 1945. 12 March 1947: the magazine says the engine first ran, without bodywork; the timeline calls it the first road test; the story says the car first ran that day. The exit terms: Ludvigsen says four years without rebuilding the Scuderia or racing involvement; Ferrari's timeline says four years without using the Ferrari name with races or racing cars; the story combines the two. Cortese's warning and the Maranello move rest on Richard Williams in Motor Sport (2014), with Jenkinson (1988) independently confirming wartime government work and the Maranello factory. Dates: Ferrari's own magazine gives the engine's first run as 12 March 1947, the Piacenza debut as 11 May and the Rome Grand Prix as 25 May; the Motor Web Museum page wrongly puts the Piacenza debut in March and is not cited for dates; some secondary pages give a different Rome date, so the story keeps Ferrari's. Win counts disagree: ferrari.com's 125 S page says six wins in 13 races over the four months after Piacenza, while the Rome article says 'six more victories' that year after Rome; the story names only the wins Motor Sport lists and uses the 13 races only in the connection. Ferrari quotations: 'a promising failure' is from ferrari.com (two pages); the settlement and 'built too hastily' lines are Ferrari's memoir as quoted by Ludvigsen. ferrari.com blocks automated requests, so its pages are cited through Internet Archive copies. Colombo's design is often credited in part to Busso, Bazzi and later Lampredi; the story names only Colombo, as both Ferrari and Motor Sport do. The Rosso Automobili page is used only as a cross-check of the Piacenza retirement.
